lessons.title: What fish need from their feed
lessons.html:
Why feed matters

Fish in a dam or tank cannot find enough food by themselves. The farm must give them feed. Feed is also the biggest cost on most fish farms. Good feeding means fast growth, healthy fish and less waste. Bad feeding means slow growth, dirty water and lost money.

The main parts of fish feed

  • Protein builds muscle and helps young fish grow. Small fish need more protein than big fish.
  • Fats (lipids) give energy.
  • Carbohydrates also give energy and help bind the pellet.
  • Vitamins and minerals keep fish healthy and help bones and scales form.

Different fish, different feed

On South African farms you will often work with tilapia, catfish (barbel) or trout. Tilapia can eat plant material and algae, so their feed has less protein. Trout eat other animals in nature, so trout feed has much more protein and fat. Always use the feed the farm manager has chosen for that species and size.

Feed sizes

Feed comes in sizes: fine crumble or powder for fry, small pellets for fingerlings and bigger pellets for grow-out fish. A pellet must fit easily into the fish's mouth. If the pellet is too big, small fish cannot eat it and it sinks and rots. If it is too small, big fish waste energy chasing many tiny bits.

Floating and sinking pellets

Floating pellets let you see the fish eat. This helps you know when they are full. Sinking pellets are used for fish that feed at the bottom. With sinking feed you must watch more carefully, because you cannot see what is left.

Natural food also helps. In earth ponds, algae and small water animals grow when the water is fertile. This natural food adds to the pellets but does not replace them.

lessons.title: Feeding fish the right way
lessons.html:
Follow the feeding plan

The farm manager makes a feeding plan. It says how much feed each tank or pond gets each day. The amount depends on the number of fish, their size and the water temperature. Your job is to follow the plan and report what you see.

Temperature and appetite

Fish are cold-blooded. When water is cold, they eat less. When water warms up, they eat more. Tilapia eat very little in winter. Trout stop eating well when water gets too warm. On cold mornings or very hot days, fish may not eat all the feed. Never force extra feed into the water.

How to feed

  1. Weigh or measure the feed for the tank. Use the scoop or scale the farm gives you.
  2. Feed at the times on the plan. Many farms feed two to four times a day.
  3. Throw feed slowly, spread over the water, not in one heap.
  4. Watch the fish. Strong splashing means they are hungry.
  5. Stop when the fish slow down and pellets stay floating.
  6. Write down how much was fed and how the fish ate.

Signs of a problem

  • Fish do not come up to eat.
  • Uneaten pellets on the bottom or along the edges.
  • Fish gasping at the surface.

Report these signs to your supervisor at once. Do not keep feeding. Uneaten feed rots and uses up oxygen in the water. This can kill fish.

Storing feed

  • Keep bags off the floor on pallets, in a dry, cool, shaded store.
  • Keep rats, birds and water away.
  • Use old stock first: first in, first out.
  • Do not use feed that is wet, mouldy or smells bad.

Lift bags with a straight back and bent knees. Ask for help with heavy loads.

Key points

  • Feed is the biggest cost, so never waste it.
  • Use the right feed type and pellet size for the fish.
  • Fish eat less in cold water; do not overfeed.
  • Uneaten feed spoils water and uses oxygen.
  • Store feed dry, off the floor, first in, first out.
